details:
**Carnaval**
Schumann's piano suite of 21 short pieces depicting a masked ball before Lent. Its movements portray real and imaginary figures, including "Florestan," "Eusebius," "Chiarina" (his future wife Clara), "Chopin," and "Paganini," and it quotes his earlier piano work Papillons. It ends with the "March of the League of David against the Philistines."

**Scenes from Childhood (Kinderszenen)**
A suite of short, simple piano pieces about childhood. It opens with "Of Foreign Lands and Peoples" and includes "Blind Man's Bluff," "Knight of the Hobbyhorse," and "The Poet Speaks." Vladimir Horowitz famously played a piece from it at his 1986 Moscow recital.

**"Träumerei" ("Dreaming")**
The famous dreamy seventh piece of Scenes from Childhood, in F major. Its melody rises gently over soft chords, and it is one of the most familiar piano pieces of the Romantic era.

**"Rhenish" Symphony (Symphony No. 3)**
A five-movement symphony in E-flat major inspired by a trip Schumann and Clara took to the Rhine region. Its first and last movements are marked "Lebhaft" ("lively"). Its solemn fourth movement, marked "Feierlich," opens with trombones and horns playing a chorale in E-flat minor. That movement depicts the ceremony at Cologne Cathedral where the archbishop was elevated to cardinal.

**"Spring" Symphony (Symphony No. 1)**
Schumann's B-flat major first symphony, premiered in 1841 with Felix Mendelssohn conducting. It was inspired by a spring poem by Adolf Böttger that ends "O turn, o turn, and change your course." Its movements were originally given titles such as "Evening" and "Merry Playmates," and its finale, "In Full Bloom," borrows a melody from Kreisleriana.

**Clara Wieck**
A celebrated piano virtuoso who married Schumann in 1840 over the objections of her father, Friedrich Wieck, who had been Schumann's piano teacher. She premiered and championed many of his works, including the Piano Concerto, and is portrayed in the "Chiarina" movement of Carnaval.

**Florestan and Eusebius**
Two imaginary characters Schumann used to stand for the two sides of his personality: the passionate, impulsive Florestan and the dreamy, introspective Eusebius. They have their own movements in Carnaval and sign the pieces of the Davidsbündlertänze. They also appear in his music criticism, where his review of Chopin's early work includes the line "Hats off, gentlemen, a genius!"

**A-S-C-H motif**
A musical code used throughout Carnaval. The letters spell Asch, the Bohemian hometown of his then-fiancée Ernestine von Fricken, and are played as the notes A–E-flat–C–B or A-flat–C–B (in German note names, Es = E-flat, As = A-flat, H = B). The letters also appear in his own name, SCHumAnn. The note groups are printed in Carnaval as "Sphinxes," which are usually left out in performance.

**Dichterliebe ("A Poet's Love")**
A cycle of 16 songs setting poems by Heinrich Heine, written in 1840, his "Year of Song." It opens with "Im wunderschönen Monat Mai" ("In the lovely month of May") and includes "Ich grolle nicht" ("I bear no grudge, though my heart is breaking"). It ends with the speaker burying his old, bad songs in a huge coffin. That same year he also wrote two Liederkreis cycles, one of them on nine Heine poems.

**Album for the Young**
A collection of easy piano pieces written in 1848 for his daughters. It includes "The Happy Farmer," "The Wild Horseman," and "Knecht Ruprecht."

**Kreisleriana**
A piano cycle named for Johannes Kreisler, the moody, antisocial musician created by E. T. A. Hoffmann. Schumann dedicated it to Chopin, who reportedly liked only the title page.

**Rhine suicide attempt and asylum**
In 1854, suffering from severe mental illness, Schumann tried to drown himself by jumping into the Rhine. He was then placed in an asylum at Endenich, where he died in 1856. His Ghost Variations, his last piano work, date from just before the attempt.

**Piano Concerto in A minor**
Schumann's only piano concerto, which, like Grieg's, is in A minor. It began as a one-movement "Phantasie" for Clara. Its first movement is marked "Allegro affettuoso," and its middle "Intermezzo: Andantino grazioso" features the cellos and leads directly into the finale.

**League of David (Davidsbündler)**
An imaginary society Schumann created to fight the "Philistines" of shallow musical taste. It gives its name to his 18-piece Davidsbündlertänze and to the finale of Carnaval, which quotes the traditional "Grandfather's Dance." He spread its ideas through the New Journal for Music (Neue Zeitschrift für Musik), which he co-founded with Friedrich Wieck and others.

**"The Two Grenadiers"**
A Schumann song setting a Heine poem about two of Napoleon's soldiers returning from Russia. It quotes "La Marseillaise" at its climax.
